    Installing and running ADMIXTURE and fastmixture

    admixture_fastmixture.Rmd

    tidygenclust estimates ancestry with the ADMIXTURE model natively, with gt_radmix(). It also provides interfaces to two external programs that fit the same model: the original ADMIXTURE program (Alexander et al. 2009), run with tidypopgen::gt_admixture(), and the python package fastmixture (Santander et al. 2024), run with gt_fastmixture(). These programs are optional: they are not needed by the rest of tidygenclust.

    In this article, we show how to install the two programs and how to run them, alongside gt_radmix(), on the dataset of the lizard Anolis punctatus (Prates et al. 2018) used in the main vignette, and we check that the three programs give consistent ancestry proportions. For a comparison of their performance, see the article “Benchmarking gt_radmix() against ADMIXTURE and fastmixture”.

    gt_radmix() estimates individual ancestry proportions (Q) and ancestral allele frequencies (P) with the method of ADMIXTURE, using a modified version of the algorithm of OpenADMIXTURE (Ko et al. 2023). Much of its C++ code is ported from the Julia implementation of OpenADMIXTURE, OpenADMIXTURE.jl, so no Julia or Python is needed. It differs from OpenADMIXTURE, hence its different name: it does not include the selection of ancestry informative markers; we implemented the cross-validation of ADMIXTURE, to choose K, which is not part of OpenADMIXTURE; it supports pseudohaploid data; and it changes some details of the computations (see ?gt_radmix). If you use it, please cite Ko et al. (2023) for the algorithm, as well as Alexander et al. (2009) for the method. If you use fastmixture, cite Santander et al. (2024), and if you use ADMIXTURE, Alexander et al. (2009).

    Installing ADMIXTURE and fastmixture

    We use reticulate to install the two programs in a conda environment (ctidygenclust; on macOS, ADMIXTURE is installed in an environment of its own, cadmixture86), so you, as a user, should not need to worry about the details of the python packages or their dependencies. This works on Linux and macOS, but NOT on Windows (where you can use the WSL). You can install both programs with:

    library(tidygenclust)
tgc_tools_install()

    or choose which programs to install, e.g. only fastmixture:

    tgc_tools_install(tools = "fastmixture")

    Programs can be added later to an existing environment with tgc_fastmixture_install() and tgc_admixture_install():

    tgc_admixture_install()

    For macOS users

    If you want to install fastmixture, you need llvm installed via brew in the first place. In bash, you will need:

    # llvm can be installed via brew
brew install llvm libomp

    Checking which programs are installed

    tgc_tools_version() reports which programs are installed (NA for those that are not):

    library(tidypopgen)
#> Loading required package: dplyr
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
#> Loading required package: tibble
library(tidygenclust)

tools_version <- tgc_tools_version()
tools_version
#> $fastmixture
#> [1] "v1.3.0"
#> 
#> $admixture
#> [1] "1.3.0"

    The code that runs each program in this article is only run if that program is available, and the comparison only if both are:

    fastmixture_available <- !is.na(tools_version$fastmixture)
admixture_available <- !is.na(tools_version$admixture)
all_available <- fastmixture_available && admixture_available

    The data

    We read the vcf file of the 46 lizards into a gen_tibble, add the population information, and group the individuals by the three genetic groups found by Prates et al. (2018): Eastern Amazonia (Eam), Western Amazonia (Wam) and the Atlantic Forest (AF):

    vcf_path <- system.file(
  "/extdata/anolis/punctatus_t70_s10_n46_filtered.recode.vcf.gz",
  package = "tidypopgen"
)
anole_gt <- gen_tibble(vcf_path,
  quiet = TRUE, backingfile = tempfile("anolis_"),
  parser = "cpp"
)
pops_path <- system.file("/extdata/anolis/punctatus_n46_meta.csv",
  package = "tidypopgen"
)
pops <- utils::read.csv(pops_path)
anole_gt <- anole_gt %>%
  left_join(pops, by = "id") %>%
  group_by(pop)
anole_gt
#> # A gen_tibble: 3249 loci

    For each program, we make a single run for K = 3.

    Running gt_radmix() 

    anole_radmix <- gt_radmix(anole_gt, k = 3, seed = 1)
summary(anole_radmix)
#> Admixture results for k =  3 
#> with slots:
#> $Q for Q matrices
#> $P for  matrices
#> $log for logs from the algorithm

    The results are stored in a gt_admix object, so we can use all the methods from tidypopgen (see the main vignette).

    Running fastmixture

    gt_fastmixture() runs fastmixture on a gen_tibble (reading its backing file directly) or on a set of PLINK files. Its arguments follow those of fastmixture, so some differ from those of gt_radmix(): the number of cores is set with threads, and cross-validation with cv, the number of folds. By default, it only returns the Q matrices (set no_freqs = FALSE to also keep the P matrices). As the fastmixture program does, it starts from a randomised SVD of the genotypes, which needs all the loci to be polymorphic (random_init = TRUE starts from random values instead, but can take much longer to converge). fastmixture prints its progress, which we hide here:

    anole_fm <- gt_fastmixture(anole_gt, k = 3, seed = 1)
    summary(anole_fm)
#> Admixture results for k =  3 
#> with slots:
#> $Q for Q matrices

    Running ADMIXTURE

    tidypopgen::gt_admixture() runs the original ADMIXTURE program: it writes the gen_tibble to PLINK files, runs ADMIXTURE on them, and reads its results back into a gt_admix object, with the log-likelihood and the log of each run. With conda_env = "auto" (the default), it uses the ADMIXTURE installed by tgc_tools_install():

    anole_adm <- gt_admixture(anole_gt, k = 3, seed = 1)
summary(anole_adm)
#> Admixture results for k =  3 
#> with slots:
#> $Q for Q matrices
#> $P for  matrices
#> $log for logs from the algorithm

    Comparing the results

    All three programs return gt_admix objects, which can be plotted with autoplot(). The labels of the clusters are arbitrary, so we first match the clusters of gt_radmix() and fastmixture to those of ADMIXTURE, so that each cluster has the same colour in all the plots:

    # all permutations of 1:n
permutations <- function(n) {
  if (n == 1) {
    return(matrix(1))
  }
  sub <- permutations(n - 1)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
    cbind(i, matrix(setdiff(seq_len(n), i)[sub], nrow = nrow(sub)))
  }))
}
# reorder the clusters of a gt_admix object with a single run, to best
# match those of the Q matrix q_ref
match_clusters <- function(adm, q_ref) {
  q <- unclass(adm$Q[[1]])
  perms <- permutations(ncol(q))
  diffs <- apply(perms, 1, function(x) sum(abs(q[, x] - q_ref)))
  best <- perms[which.min(diffs), ]
  adm$Q[[1]] <- q_matrix(q[, best])
  if (!is.null(adm$P)) {
    adm$P[[1]] <- adm$P[[1]][, best]
  }
  adm
}
q_adm <- unclass(anole_adm$Q[[1]])
anole_radmix <- match_clusters(anole_radmix, q_adm)
anole_fm <- match_clusters(anole_fm, q_adm)
    library(ggplot2)
plots <- list(
  autoplot(anole_radmix, type = "barplot", k = 3, run = 1,
    annotate_group = TRUE
  ) +
    ggtitle("gt_radmix"),
  autoplot(anole_fm, type = "barplot", k = 3, run = 1,
    annotate_group = TRUE
  ) +
    ggtitle("fastmixture"),
  autoplot(anole_adm, type = "barplot", k = 3, run = 1,
    annotate_group = TRUE
  ) +
    ggtitle("ADMIXTURE")
)
patchwork::wrap_plots(plots, ncol = 1)

    The three plots look the same. To confirm it, we compare the ancestry proportions of each individual with those estimated by ADMIXTURE:

    q_differences <- function(adm) {
  q <- unclass(adm$Q[[1]])
  c(
    max_abs_difference = max(abs(q - q_adm)),
    correlation = stats::cor(as.vector(q), as.vector(q_adm))
  )
}
rbind(
  gt_radmix = q_differences(anole_radmix),
  fastmixture = q_differences(anole_fm)
)
#>             max_abs_difference correlation
#> gt_radmix          0.004659000   0.9999983
#> fastmixture        0.005003754   0.9999981

    Cross-validation

    To choose K, all three programs can compute a cross-validation error for each run, with crossval = TRUE in gt_radmix() and gt_admixture(), and with cv (the number of folds) in gt_fastmixture():

    gt_radmix(anole_gt, k = 2:4, n_runs = 3, crossval = TRUE)
gt_admixture(anole_gt, k = 2:4, n_runs = 3, crossval = TRUE)
gt_fastmixture(anole_gt, k = 2:4, n_runs = 3, cv = 5)

    gt_radmix() implements the procedure of ADMIXTURE, which hides random genotypes, whereas fastmixture hides whole individuals: its errors are on a different scale, and only the value of K that they favour can be compared with those of the other two programs.

    References

    Alexander DH, Novembre J, Lange K (2009) Fast model-based estimation of ancestry in unrelated individuals. Genome Research, 19(9), 1655-1664.

    Ko S, Chu BB, Peterson D, Okenwa C, Papp JC, Alexander DH, Sobel EM, Zhou H, Lange KL (2023) Unsupervised discovery of ancestry informative markers and genetic admixture proportions in biobank-scale datasets. The American Journal of Human Genetics, 110(2), 314-325.

    Prates I, Penna A, Rodrigues MT, Carnaval AC (2018) Local adaptation in mainland anole lizards: Integrating population history and genome-environment associations. Ecology and Evolution, 8(23), 11932-11944.

    Santander CG, Refoyo Martinez A, Meisner J (2024) Faster model-based estimation of ancestry proportions. Peer Community Journal, 4: e115. https://doi.org/10.24072/pcjournal.503
